pdm-ecg: Which property refers to a cardiac cell's ability to produce its own impulse?
Automaticity
What does depolarization represent, and what is its relationship to contraction?
Activation of cardiac tissue, and it precedes contraction
In what order do the five phases of the cardiac action potential occur?
Phase 4, then 0, 1, 2 and 3
What is the ionic arrangement during phase 4, the resting state?
More potassium inside the cell
What happens during phase 0, the upstroke?
Fast sodium channels open and sodium rushes into the cell
What characterizes phase 1, early repolarization?
Sodium channels close and potassium channels reopen
Why is phase 2 called the plateau?
Calcium entering the cell is matched by potassium moving the other way
Over which part of the action potential does the ABSOLUTE refractory period run?
From phase 0 to the middle of phase 3
Where does the sinoatrial node sit?
In the upper wall of the right atrium
Which internodal tract does the majority of the population use?
The superior anterior, or fast, tract
What two things does the atrioventricular node do to the impulse passing through it?
It introduces a short pause and amplifies the signal
What is distinctive about the bundle of His in a normal heart?
It is the only electrical pathway crossing from the atria to the ventricles
Into how many fascicles does the left bundle branch divide, and what are they?
Three: left anterior, left posterior and septal
What does a cardiac vector represent?
The direction and strength of the electrical impulse
What does a BIPOLAR lead measure?
The voltage difference between two distinct body points
Why are the augmented leads considered unipolar?
Only one physical electrode is used
A standard twelve-lead electrocardiogram uses how many physical electrodes?
Ten
Which six electrocardiographic leads do the four limb electrodes produce?
Leads I, II and III together with aVR, aVL and aVF
What is the hexaxial reference system used to determine?
The normal axis of the heart
What view of the heart do the precordial leads give?
A horizontal view
What are contiguous leads?
Two or more leads looking at the same area of the heart
The overall vector at a given moment is directed away from a lead. What does that lead record?
A negative deflection
How much time does one small box on electrocardiogram paper represent?
0.04 seconds
Why is lead II used for rhythm interpretation?
It has a near-perfect view along the heart's vector
What distinguishes a SEGMENT from an INTERVAL?
A segment is the flat line between two waves
What does the P wave represent, and how should it appear in lead II?
Atrial depolarization, appearing as a positive deflection
A PR interval measures seven small boxes. How should that be read?
Prolonged, since the normal range is three to five small boxes
What does the QRS complex represent, and what should it look like?
Ventricular depolarization, narrow with sharp points
What does the R wave represent?
Depolarization of the anterior left ventricle
What must a deflection do to count as a true S wave?
Extend below the baseline
What is the J point?
The junction where the QRS complex ends and the ST segment begins
What is happening mechanically during the ST segment?
The ventricles are holding their contraction to allow emptying
What does the peak of the T wave mark?
The dividing line between the absolute and the relative refractory period
What does the QT interval span?
From the start of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave
pdm-cardiac-imaging: What is the standing of chest radiography in cardiac evaluation?
It is not the primary modality, but it gives useful clues when obtained
Why does the cardiothoracic ratio require a properly performed posteroanterior film?
Projection alters the apparent size of the cardiac silhouette
What is cephalization on a chest radiograph?
Upper zone vessels becoming larger
How does a vascular ultrasound image form?
Quartz crystals emit pulses that reflect off tissue
What does echocardiography evaluate?
Chamber size, ventricular function, valves, shunts and pressures
Name four types of stress test.
Exercise, echocardiographic, nuclear, pharmacological
How does an exercise stress test detect myocardial ischemia?
Indirectly, by continuous electrocardiographic monitoring
For which patient is an echocardiographic stress test the appropriate initial choice?
One who can exercise but whose resting tracing is abnormal
Which patients receive a pharmacological rather than an exercise stress test?
Those who cannot exercise
Why are cardiac medications given before a cardiac computed tomography study?
To control heart rate, since the moving heart degrades the images
How does nuclear perfusion imaging compare with standard and echocardiographic stress testing?
Its sensitivity and specificity are superior
What does cardiovascular magnetic resonance avoid that computed tomography does not?
Both ionizing radiation and iodinated contrast
What does electrophysiological testing do?
Investigates rhythm disorders and locates an arrhythmia
What is coronary angiography the gold standard for?
Coronary artery anatomy and cardiac function
What does LEFT heart catheterization assess?
Coronary anatomy, aortic pressure and left ventricular function
Which structures can be at least partly seen on a chest radiograph for cardiac purposes?
Cardiac silhouette, great vessels, lungs and pleura
In which patients is cephalization seen?
Heart failure and pulmonary hypertension
On a vascular ultrasound, how does tissue density relate to the image?
The denser the structure the lighter it appears
What distinguishes a transthoracic from a transesophageal echocardiogram?
The transducer is outside the body in one, inside in the other
Which electrocardiographic changes during an exercise stress test suggest ischemia?
ST depression
What is the echocardiogram looking for after exercise, and why must it be obtained quickly?
Abnormal left ventricular wall motion induced by exercise
What is a non-contrast cardiac computed tomography particularly useful for?
Coronary artery calcium scoring
How is the heart stressed for a nuclear perfusion study in a patient who cannot exercise?
Pharmacologically, with an agent such as adenosine
What is done before a cardiovascular magnetic resonance study is ordered?
An echocardiogram
What does catheter ablation do during electrophysiological testing?
Inactivates part of the heart by destroying that tissue
Which is an indication for coronary angiography?
Severe angina despite medical therapy
What does RIGHT heart catheterization assess?
Right-sided pressures, pulmonary resistance, valves and shunts
Which chest radiograph findings indicate cardiac pathology?
Edema, effusion, cardiomegaly, cephalization and calcification
How are veins and arteries told apart on a vascular ultrasound?
Veins collapse when compressed and arteries pulsate
Why is transthoracic echocardiography the most common echo procedure?
It can be performed at the bedside and is noninvasive
Which exercise modalities are used, and which is preferred among the cycles?
Treadmill and cycle ergometer
Which is an indication for coronary computed tomography angiography?
Evaluating an equivocal or non-diagnostic stress test
pdm-cardiac-biomarkers-lipids: Which question do cardiac biomarkers answer?
Is there acute cardiac injury or stress?
Which question does a lipid profile answer?
What is the patient's long-term atherosclerotic risk?
Which biomarker is the marker of choice for myocardial necrosis?
Cardiac troponin
What troponin level supports acute myocardial infarction with ischemic symptoms?
Above the 99th percentile upper reference limit
What does the 99th percentile upper reference limit represent?
A value higher than 99% of a healthy population
Which troponin subunit has cardiac specificity?
Troponin I
Why is troponin C not used as a cardiac biomarker?
It is not specific to cardiac muscle
What does 'high-sensitivity' troponin describe?
The assay, not a different troponin subunit
When is a high-sensitivity troponin repeated after the first draw?
At 1 to 2 hours
What is the pitfall of high-sensitivity troponin?
It can detect troponin in healthy people
What separates myocardial infarction from myocardial injury?
Ischemia plus a rising or falling troponin pattern
In which conditions can troponin be chronically elevated?
Chronic kidney disease, heart failure and structural heart disease
Why is troponin preferred over creatine kinase-MB?
It rises sooner and stays elevated longer
Which three markers are no longer used to evaluate cardiac disease?
Creatine kinase-MB, myoglobin and lactate dehydrogenase
Which test evaluates suspected statin myopathy or rhabdomyolysis?
Creatine kinase
What does B-type natriuretic peptide reflect?
Myocardial wall stretch, not injury
Which natriuretic peptide fragment is biologically inert?
N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide
How does obesity affect natriuretic peptide levels?
It makes them falsely low
How does worsening kidney function affect natriuretic peptide levels?
It raises them
What is the main diagnostic use of a natriuretic peptide?
Ruling out new-onset heart failure
Where is C-reactive protein made?
In the liver, as an acute-phase reactant
Which process produces the highest C-reactive protein levels?
Bacterial infection
What is high-sensitivity C-reactive protein used for?
Refining cardiovascular risk, not acute diagnosis
Name a drug class that lowers C-reactive protein.
Statins
Which biomarker is an input to the Reynolds Risk Score?
High-sensitivity C-reactive protein
Which troponin rise defines a bypass-related (type 5) infarction?
More than 10 times the 99th percentile limit
What does a late troponin elevation at 4 weeks relate to?
Lower left ventricular ejection fraction
Why do cholesterol and triglycerides travel in lipoproteins?
They are insoluble in plasma
What makes up a lipoprotein?
A lipid core, a phospholipid shell and apolipoproteins
What is LDL (low-density lipoprotein) derived from?
VLDL (very low-density lipoprotein) after triglyceride is stripped
Which apolipoprotein do chylomicrons carry?
Apolipoprotein B-48, made by the intestine
Which apolipoprotein is absent from HDL (high-density lipoprotein)?
Apolipoprotein B
What is the major structural protein of HDL (high-density lipoprotein)?
Apolipoprotein A-I
Which apolipoprotein is critical in triglyceride clearance?
Apolipoprotein E
Which lipoprotein is the principal driver of atherosclerosis?
LDL (low-density lipoprotein)
What does HDL (high-density lipoprotein) perform?
Reverse cholesterol transport
What is lipoprotein(a)?
An LDL-like particle with apolipoprotein(a) bound to apolipoprotein B-100
How often is lipoprotein(a) generally measured?
Once in a lifetime
Does a statin lower lipoprotein(a)?
No
Which lipid panel components are measured directly?
Total cholesterol, HDL (high-density lipoprotein) cholesterol and triglycerides
How is non-HDL (non-high-density lipoprotein) cholesterol derived?
Total cholesterol minus HDL (high-density lipoprotein) cholesterol
When can the Friedewald equation not be used?
When triglycerides are 400 mg/dL or above
What is the Friedewald equation?
Total cholesterol minus HDL (high-density lipoprotein) cholesterol minus triglycerides divided by 5
What acute risk comes with triglycerides of 500 mg/dL or above?
Pancreatitis
How is a low HDL (high-density lipoprotein) cholesterol used?
As a risk marker, not a treatment target
Which lipid values have risk-based goals rather than one normal value?
LDL (low-density lipoprotein) cholesterol and non-HDL (non-high-density lipoprotein) cholesterol
When is a fasting lipid profile needed?
Triglycerides 400 or above, a triglyceride disorder, or family history of premature disease
At what ages are children routinely screened for lipids?
Ages 9 to 11
How often are adults screened for lipids?
About every 5 years from age 19
When are lipids rechecked after starting a statin?
In 4 to 12 weeks
What reclassifies risk at borderline or intermediate tier when uncertain?
A coronary artery calcium score
What does an elevated lipoprotein(a) prompt?
Earlier, more intensive control of other risk factors
